content.text:
6 Constructions and Tilings
6.1 Geometric Constructions
Eyes
Do you recall the 'Eyes' construction we did in Grade 6?
Of course, eyes can be drawn freehand, but we wanted to construct them so that the lower arc and upper arc of each eye look symmetrical. We relied on our spatial estimation to determine the two centres, A and B (see the figure), from which we drew the lower arc and upper arc respectively.
The arcs define a line XY that 'supports' the drawing though it is not part of the final figure. We can start with this supporting line and systematically find the centres A and B.

content.text:

2. Make a guess before the next step: where must the compass point be placed for each arc, so that both arcs pass through X and Y and the eye looks the same above and below?

media.title: Equal Distance Finder
media.context: Class 7 NCERT Ganita Prakash ch 14 Constructions and Tilings (Equal Distances: the Perpendicular Bisector). Slide P. Find points equally far from X and Y. Viral_V3 tool, ported from its standalone HTML.
media.description: Equal Distance Finder. Slide P. Find points equally far from X and Y. Authored rounds, no modes and no question bank: the child acts on the board, then answers; a header with points, hint, sound and home; a task card with Check; a message pill; step dots; Next / Finish; a finish screen with stars. Everything starts raw and changes only when the child acts. English, Hindi and Gujarati.

tool_config.idea: Every point that is the same distance from X and Y lies on one straight line: the perpendicular bisector of XY. The student discovers the line by placing points, not by being told.
tool_config.title: Equal Distance Finder
tool_config.screen: A segment XY on a grid; a draggable point P with live distances PX and PY; a Drop button that leaves a dot where PX equals PY; a toggle that draws the line through the dropped dots and marks its angle with XY.
feedback: A dropped dot where PX and PY differ is refused, with both distances shown in red.
When five dots line up, the line appears and the right angle mark flashes at the midpoint.
A point off the line shows which of X and Y it is nearer to.
tool_config.done_when: Six challenges done, with the line drawn and the 90° named.
challenges: XY of 6 cm: drop five equal-distance points.
Find the equal-distance point that lies on XY itself (the midpoint).
Find two equal-distance points 5 cm from X and Y (one on each side).
XY turned slanting: drop equal-distance points again.
Test a point 4 cm from X and 5 cm from Y: is it on the line?
Say the angle between the line and XY (90°).

hint_ladder.text: What must be true of PX and PY for a dot to be accepted?
Find the midpoint first, then look for equal-distance points straight above and below it.
Keep P on the line through the midpoint at a right angle to XY and watch the two distances.
All equal-distance points lie on the perpendicular bisector: through the midpoint, at 90° to XY.

student_does: Drag P until PX and PY read the same, then drop a dot.
Drop at least five such dots, above and below XY.
Predict the shape the dots make before turning on the line.
Check where the line meets XY and the angle it makes.

content.text:
For the eye to be symmetrical, or for the supporting line to be the line of symmetry, the upper and lower arcs should have the same radius. In other words, we must have AX = BX. Since AX = AY and BX = BY, this means AX = AY = BX = BY.
How do we find such A and B?
From X and Y, draw arcs above and below XY, with the same radii. The two points at which the arcs meet, above and below XY, give us A and B, respectively.
Use this to construct an eye.
Join A and B with a line. Where does AB intersect XY, and what is the angle formed between them?
We observe that AB passes through the midpoint of XY, and is also perpendicular to it.
A division of a line, or any geometrical object, into two identical parts is called bisection. A line that bisects a given line and is perpendicular to it, is called the perpendicular bisector.

content.text:
Will the line joining the two points at which the arcs meet, above and below XY, always be the perpendicular bisector of XY, i.e., when XY is of any length, and the arcs are drawn using a radius of any length?
This can be answered through congruence. Let us consider a line segment XY. Find points A and B such that AX = AY = BX = BY. Draw the lines AB, AX, AY, BX and BY. Let O be the point of intersection between AB and XY.
Which two triangles should be congruent for AB to be the perpendicular bisector of XY (that is, O is the midpoint of XY and AB is perpendicular to XY)?
If we show that ΔAOX ≅ ΔAOY, then OX = OY, and ∠AOX = ∠AOY because they are corresponding parts of congruent triangles. Since ∠AOX and ∠AOY together form a straight angle, we have ∠AOX + ∠AOY = 180°. Thus, ∠AOX = ∠AOY = 90°. This establishes that O is the midpoint of XY and AB is perpendicular to XY.
In ΔAOX and ΔAOY, we already know that AX = AY, and AO is common to both triangles.
If we can show that ∠XAO = ∠YAO then, by the SAS congruence condition, we can conclude that the triangles are congruent.
To show this, we observe that ΔABX ≅ ΔABY. This is so because AX = AY, BX = BY, and AB is common to both the triangles.
Thus, we have ∠XAB = ∠YAB, or ∠XAO = ∠YAO because they are corresponding parts of congruent triangles.
Hence, AB is the perpendicular bisector of XY.

content.text:
Worked example: Points A and B satisfy AX = AY = BX = BY, and AB meets XY at O. Prove that O is the midpoint of XY and that AB is perpendicular to XY.
{{DIAGRAM:M1.S2.T2.C4.IMG2}}
1. In ΔABX and ΔABY: AX = AY, BX = BY, and AB is common. So ΔABX ≅ ΔABY by the SSS condition.
2. Corresponding parts are equal, so ∠XAB = ∠YAB, that is, ∠XAO = ∠YAO.
3. In ΔAOX and ΔAOY: AX = AY, ∠XAO = ∠YAO, and AO is common. So ΔAOX ≅ ΔAOY by the SAS condition.
4. Corresponding parts are equal, so OX = OY: O is the midpoint of XY.
5. Also ∠AOX = ∠AOY, and together they make a straight angle of 180°.
6. So each of ∠AOX and ∠AOY is half of 180°, which is 90°.
Answer: ΔABX ≅ ΔABY by SSS, then ΔAOX ≅ ΔAOY by SAS; so OX = OY and ∠AOX = ∠AOY = 90°: AB is the perpendicular bisector of XY

content.question: Points A and B satisfy AX = AY = BX = BY, and AB meets XY at O. Prove that O is the midpoint of XY and that AB is perpendicular to XY.
content.publication_text:
Worked example: Points A and B satisfy AX = AY = BX = BY, and AB meets XY at O. Prove that O is the midpoint of XY and that AB is perpendicular to XY.
{{DIAGRAM:M1.S2.T2.C4.IMG2}}
1. In ΔABX and ΔABY: AX = AY, BX = BY, and AB is common. So ΔABX ≅ ΔABY by the SSS condition.
2. Corresponding parts are equal, so ∠XAB = ∠YAB, that is, ∠XAO = ∠YAO.
3. In ΔAOX and ΔAOY: AX = AY, ∠XAO = ∠YAO, and AO is common. So ΔAOX ≅ ΔAOY by the SAS condition.
4. Corresponding parts are equal, so OX = OY: O is the midpoint of XY.
5. Also ∠AOX = ∠AOY, and together they make a straight angle of 180°.
6. So each of ∠AOX and ∠AOY is half of 180°, which is 90°.
Answer: ΔABX ≅ ΔABY by SSS, then ΔAOX ≅ ΔAOY by SAS; so OX = OY and ∠AOX = ∠AOY = 90°: AB is the perpendicular bisector of XY

concepts.concept_name: Why AB is the perpendicular bisector

content.text:
We can have eyes of different shapes. How do we get these different shapes? Try!
One way is to choose two other points C and D such that CX = CY = DX = DY. An eye of a different shape can be drawn using these points.
Will C and D lie on the perpendicular bisector AB?
The points C and D are at the same distance from both X and Y. We have just seen that joining any two such points gives the perpendicular bisector of XY. Since XY has only one perpendicular bisector, which is the line AB, the points C and D must lie on the line AB.
Justify the following statement using the facts that we have established. Any point that has the same distance from X and Y lies on the perpendicular bisector of XY.
Thus, eyes of different shapes can be drawn by suitably choosing different pairs of points on the perpendicular bisector as centres to construct the upper and lower arcs of the eyes.

$1$. Open the compass to a radius more than half of $XY$.

$3$. With centre $Y$ and the same radius, draw arcs that cut the first two arcs.
$4$. Name the meeting point above $XY$ as $A$ and the one below $XY$ as $B$. Then $AX = AY = BX = BY$.
$5$. With centre $A$ and radius $AX$, draw the lower arc from $X$ to $Y$.
$6$. With centre $B$ and the same radius, draw the upper arc from $X$ to $Y$. The two arcs make the eye.
Answer: $A$ and $B$ are the meeting points of equal arcs from $X$ and $Y$; the arc centred at $A$ is the lower arc and the arc centred at $B$ is the upper arc

Answer: $A$ and $B$ are the meeting points of equal arcs from $X$ and $Y$; the arc centred at $A$ is the lower arc and the arc centred at $B$ is the upper arc

content.text:
{{DIAGRAM:M1.S3.T3.C10.IMG1}}
$1$. If $P$ is on the same side of $XY$ as $A$, pair $P$ with $B$; otherwise pair $P$ with $A$. Say we pair $P$ with $B$.
$2$. Then $PX = PY$ and $BX = BY$, so $P$ and $B$ are each equally far from $X$ and $Y$.
$3$. In $\triangle PBX$ and $\triangle PBY$: $PX = PY$, $BX = BY$, and $PB$ is common, so $\triangle PBX$ is congruent to $\triangle PBY$ by $SSS$.
$4$. So $\angle XPB = \angle YPB$, and if $PB$ meets $XY$ at $O$, then $\triangle POX$ is congruent to $\triangle POY$ by $SAS$, with $PX = PY$, equal angles at $P$ and $PO$ common. So $OX = OY$ and the angles at $O$ are $90^\circ$.
$5$. So the line $PB$ is the perpendicular bisector of $XY$.
$6$. $XY$ has only one perpendicular bisector, the line $AB$, so $P$ lies on $AB$.
Answer: The line through $P$ and $B$ is the perpendicular bisector of $XY$, using $SSS$ and then $SAS$; $XY$ has only one perpendicular bisector, so $P$ lies on $AB$
steps: If P is on the same side of XY as A, pair P with B; otherwise pair P with A. Say we pair P with B.
Then PX = PY and BX = BY, so P and B are each equally far from X and Y.
In ΔPBX and ΔPBY: PX = PY, BX = BY, and PB is common, so ΔPBX ≅ ΔPBY by SSS.
So ∠XPB = ∠YPB, and if PB meets XY at O, then ΔPOX ≅ ΔPOY by SAS (PX = PY, equal angles at P, PO common). So OX = OY and the angles at O are 90°.
So the line PB is the perpendicular bisector of XY.
XY has only one perpendicular bisector, the line AB, so P lies on AB.

maths_rules: Opening r with r more than half of XY, so that arcs from X and from Y meet.
Arcs of radius r from X and Y above XY meet at A; arcs of the same radius r below XY meet at B; AX = AY = BX = BY = r.
Line AB meets XY at O; triangle ABX is congruent to triangle ABY by SSS, and triangle AOX is congruent to triangle AOY by SAS, so OX = OY and angle AOX = angle AOY = 90 degrees.
Slip: with the opening less than half of XY, the arcs from X and Y stop short of each other and do not meet, so no point A exists.

content.text:
Construction of Perpendicular Bisector
Given a line segment XY, how do we draw its perpendicular bisector using only an unmarked ruler and a compass?
We have seen that joining any two points, one above XY and one below, that are at equal distances from X and Y, gives the perpendicular bisector of XY. This gives a method to construct the perpendicular bisector.
1. Taking some fixed radius, from X and then Y, construct two sufficiently long arcs above XY. Name the point where the arcs meet as A.
2. Using the same radius, from X and then Y, construct two sufficiently long arcs below XY. Name the point where the arcs meet as B.
3. AB is the required perpendicular bisector.
Thus, the perpendicular bisector can be constructed using the simplest geometric tools, an unmarked ruler and a compass. We will use only these two tools for all the other geometric constructions in this chapter, unless there is a need for drawing lines of specific lengths in standard units.
This method of constructing the perpendicular bisector is not only geometrically exact but also a practical way to construct it accurately.
This method to find the midpoint of a line segment is more accurate than measuring the length using a marked scale.

content.text:
Worked example: Draw a line segment XY. Construct its perpendicular bisector using only an unmarked ruler and a compass, and mark the midpoint of XY.
{{DIAGRAM:M1.S4.T4.C11.IMG2}}
1. Open the compass to a radius more than half of XY, so that the arcs will meet.
2. With centre X, draw a long arc above XY. With centre Y and the same radius, draw an arc above XY that cuts it. Name the meeting point A.
3. Keep the same radius. With centres X and Y, draw two arcs below XY that cut each other at B.
4. Join A and B with the ruler. AB is the perpendicular bisector of XY.
5. Mark O where AB crosses XY. O is the midpoint of XY, and ∠AOX = 90°.
6. Reason: AX = AY and BX = BY, so ΔABX ≅ ΔABY by SSS and then ΔAOX ≅ ΔAOY by SAS.
Answer: AB, the line through the two meeting points of equal arcs, is the perpendicular bisector; it meets XY at its midpoint O

maths_rules: Radius r from X and from Y above XY, r more than half of XY, meets at A: AX = AY = r.
A different radius s from X and from Y below XY, s more than half of XY, meets at B: BX = BY = s.
Triangle ABX is congruent to triangle ABY by SSS (AX = AY, BX = BY, AB common), so angle XAO = angle YAO where AB meets XY at O.
Triangle AOX is congruent to triangle AOY by SAS (AX = AY, equal angles at A, AO common), so OX = OY and angle AOX = angle AOY = 90 degrees.
A and B are each equally far from X and Y, and two points fix one line, so line AB is the perpendicular bisector.

video_script.anchor: Can both pairs of arcs be constructed on the same side of X Y?
video_script.design: One idea: both meeting points can lie on one side if the two radii are different. The construction of the book's example is repeated, and the same two congruences explain it.

maths_rules: Radius r from X and from Y above XY, r more than half of XY, meets at A: AX = AY = r.
A larger radius s, above XY again, meets at P: PX = PY = s. If s = r the arcs meet at A again, so the radii must differ.
Triangle APX is congruent to triangle APY by SSS (AX = AY, PX = PY, AP common), so angle XAP = angle YAP.

Line AP extended meets XY at O; angle XAO = 180 degrees minus angle XAP and angle YAO = 180 degrees minus angle YAP, so they are equal. Triangle AOX is congruent to triangle AOY by SAS, so OX = OY and angle AOX = angle AOY = 90 degrees.
A and P are each equally far from X and Y, so both lie on the perpendicular bisector, and two points fix one line.
video_script.payoff_line: No, both pairs of arcs can be on the same side

final_answer.value: No. Both pairs can be on the same side if the two radii are different; each meeting point is equally far from X and Y, so both lie on the perpendicular bisector (SSS, then SAS), and the line through them, extended, is the perpendicular bisector
final_answer.spoken: no, both pairs of arcs can be on the same side, if the two radii are different, and the line through the two meeting points is the perpendicular bisector

content.text:
{{DIAGRAM:M1.S5.T5.C14.IMG1}}
$1$. Construct: arcs of radius $r$ from $X$ and $Y$ above $XY$ meet at $A$, so $AX = AY$.
$2$. Arcs of a different radius $s$ from $X$ and $Y$ below $XY$ meet at $B$, so $BX = BY$.
$3$. $A$ is equally far from $X$ and $Y$, so $A$ lies on the perpendicular bisector. $B$ is equally far from $X$ and $Y$, so $B$ lies on it too.
$4$. Why: $\triangle ABX$ is congruent to $\triangle ABY$ by $SSS$, with $AX = AY$, $BX = BY$ and $AB$ common, so $\angle XAO = \angle YAO$; then $\triangle AOX$ is congruent to $\triangle AOY$ by $SAS$, with $AX = AY$, equal angles at $A$ and $AO$ common, so $OX = OY$ and $\angle AOX = \angle AOY = 90^\circ$.
$5$. Two points fix a whole line, so $AB$ is the perpendicular bisector.
Answer: No. The radius above may differ from the radius below; $A$ and $B$ are each equally far from $X$ and $Y$, so both lie on the perpendicular bisector, using $SSS$ and then $SAS$, and two points fix the line

Two points fix a whole line, so AB is the perpendicular bisector.

content.text:
{{DIAGRAM:M1.S5.T5.C16.IMG1}}
$1$. Construct: arcs of radius $r$ from $X$ and $Y$ above $XY$ meet at $A$.
$2$. Arcs of a larger radius $s$ from $X$ and $Y$, also above $XY$, meet at a second point $P$. The radii must differ, or the arcs meet again at $A$.
$3$. $AX = AY$ and $PX = PY$, so $A$ and $P$ are each equally far from $X$ and $Y$.
$4$. Why: by $SSS$, $\triangle APX$ is congruent to $\triangle APY$, with $AX = AY$, $PX = PY$ and $AP$ common, so line $AP$ makes equal angles with $AX$ and $AY$; then $SAS$ on the triangles at the meeting point $O$ gives $OX = OY$ and two $90^\circ$ angles.
$5$. So the line $AP$, extended to cross $XY$, is the perpendicular bisector.
Answer: No. Both pairs can be on the same side if the two radii are different; each meeting point is equally far from $X$ and $Y$, so both lie on the perpendicular bisector, using $SSS$ and then $SAS$, and the line through them, extended, is the perpendicular bisector

So the line AP, extended to cross XY, is the perpendicular bisector.

media.description: A point O is marked on a line, and a ninety degree angle is built at O with a ruler and a compass. Equal marks on both sides make O a midpoint, and one pair of arcs gives the perpendicular bisector. Keeko's doubt, that two pairs of arcs are needed, is answered by pointing out that O already lies on the bisector.

video_script.design: One idea: make O the midpoint of X Y, and the perpendicular bisector passes through O, so one pair of arcs is enough. Kiko's doubt is the book's own question, whether two pairs of arcs are needed.

video_script.wrong_move: Kiko draws one pair of arcs above the line and a second pair below it, as in the perpendicular bisector, before joining the points.
maths_rules: Arcs from O with one radius cut the line at X and Y: OX = OY, so O is the midpoint of XY.
Arcs of a wider radius from X and from Y meet at A above the line: AX = AY.
Triangle AOX is congruent to triangle AOY by SSS (AX = AY, OX = OY, AO common), so angle AOX = angle AOY.
Angle AOX + angle AOY = 180 degrees (straight angle), so each is 180 / 2 = 90 degrees.
Slip: a radius equal to OX from X and from Y gives arcs that meet only at O, so there is no new point above the line, or a second pair below is drawn when O is already on the bisector.

final_answer.value: ∠AOX = 90°, since ΔAOX ≅ ΔAOY by SSS and the two equal angles make a straight angle

content.text:
Construction of a 90° Angle at a Given Point
Can we extend the method of constructing the perpendicular bisector to construct a 90° angle at any point on a line? Draw a line and mark a point O on it. Construct a 90° angle at point O.
Find a segment of this line for which O is the midpoint.
Extend the line on either side of O. Using a compass, mark two points X and Y at equal distance from O, so that O is the midpoint of XY.
The perpendicular bisector of XY will pass through O and is perpendicular to the given line.
In this case, do we need to draw two pairs of intersecting arcs to get the perpendicular bisector of XY?
No, we don't. We already have one point, O, lying on the perpendicular bisector.

content.text:
1. Predict first: we already know one point of the perpendicular bisector. How many more points do we need?
2. With centre O, cut the line at X and Y, so that OX = OY and O is the midpoint of XY.
3. With a larger radius, draw arcs from X and Y on one side; they meet at A. Then AX = AY.
4. Join OA. ΔAOX ≅ ΔAOY by SSS, so ∠AOX = ∠AOY, and they make 180°, so each is 90°.

Join it to O: ΔAOX ≅ ΔAOY by SSS, so the angle at O is 90°.

content.text:
{{DIAGRAM:M1.S7.T7.C22.IMG1}}
$1$. With centre $O$ and any radius, draw arcs that cut the line at $X$ and at $Y$. Then $OX = OY$.
$2$. Open the compass wider than $OX$. With centre $X$, draw an arc above the line.
$3$. With centre $Y$ and the same radius, draw an arc that cuts it at $A$. Then $AX = AY$.
$4$. Join $O$ and $A$. $\angle AOX$ is the required $90^\circ$ angle.
$5$. Reason: in $\triangle AOX$ and $\triangle AOY$, $AX = AY$, $OX = OY$, and $AO$ is common, so $\triangle AOX$ is congruent to $\triangle AOY$ by $SSS$.
$6$. So $\angle AOX = \angle AOY$. Together they make $180^\circ$, so each is $90^\circ$.
Answer: $\angle AOX = 90^\circ$, since $\triangle AOX$ is congruent to $\triangle AOY$ by $SSS$ and the two equal angles make a straight angle
steps: With centre O and any radius, draw arcs that cut the line at X and at Y. Then OX = OY.
Open the compass wider than OX. With centre X, draw an arc above the line.
With centre Y and the same radius, draw an arc that cuts it at A. Then AX = AY.
Join O and A. ∠AOX is the required 90° angle.
Reason: in ΔAOX and ΔAOY, AX = AY, OX = OY, and AO is common, so ΔAOX ≅ ΔAOY by SSS.
So ∠AOX = ∠AOY. Together they make 180°, so each is 90°.
content.answer: ∠AOX = 90°, since ΔAOX ≅ ΔAOY by SSS and the two equal angles make a straight angle

maths_rules: An arc with centre O cuts OY at A and OX at B: OA = OB.
Arcs of one radius from A and from B, long enough to meet inside the angle, meet at C: AC = BC.
In triangles OAC and OBC: OA = OB, AC = BC, OC common, so triangle OAC is congruent to triangle OBC by SSS.
So angle AOC = angle BOC, and OC bisects angle XOY.
Slip: radii r from A and R from B with R more than r meet at a point C with AC = r and BC = R, so AC is not equal to BC and the triangles do not match.

content.text:
We will now develop a general method to bisect any angle. Consider an angle ∠XOY.
We can bisect it if we can draw two congruent triangles ΔOBC and ΔOAC as shown in the figure. Then ∠BOC = ∠AOC.
How do we construct these congruent triangles, given the angle?
If A and B are marked such that OA = OB, and if C is chosen such that BC = AC, then by the SSS congruence condition, ΔOBC ≅ ΔOAC. So we can bisect an angle as follows.
Steps for Angle Bisection
1. Mark points A and B such that OA = OB.
2. Choosing any sufficiently long radius, cut arcs from A and B, keeping the radius same. Mark the point of intersection as C.
3. OC bisects ∠AOB.

content.text:
Worked example: Draw any angle ∠XOY. Bisect it using only a ruler and a compass, and justify that the two parts are equal.
{{DIAGRAM:M2.S8.T8.C23.IMG2}}
1. With centre O and any radius, draw an arc that cuts OY at A and OX at B. Then OA = OB.
2. With centre A and a radius long enough for the arcs to meet, draw an arc inside the angle.
3. With centre B and the same radius, draw an arc that cuts it at C. Then AC = BC.
4. Join O and C.
5. In ΔOAC and ΔOBC: OA = OB, AC = BC, and OC is common. So ΔOAC ≅ ΔOBC by SSS.
6. So ∠AOC = ∠BOC, and OC bisects ∠XOY.
Answer: OC bisects ∠XOY, because ΔOAC ≅ ΔOBC by SSS

content.text:
Angle Bisection for a Design
How do we construct this figure? (Eight equal petals meet at one centre.)
The supporting lines for this figure will look like this.
What is the angle between two adjacent lines?
We need the angle between every pair of adjacent lines to be equal. Since 360° is equally divided into 8 parts, every angle is 45°.
How do we construct a 45° angle using only a ruler and a compass?
We know how to construct a 90° angle. If we can divide it into two equal parts, or bisect it, then we get a 45° angle.
So, a 45° angle can be constructed by first constructing a 90° angle and then bisecting it.

content.text:
Worked example: Eight equal petals meet at a centre, along eight equally spaced supporting lines. Find the angle between neighbouring lines, and construct it with a ruler and a compass.
{{DIAGRAM:M2.S8.T8.C24.IMG2}}
1. The eight angles round the centre are equal and make a full turn of 360°.
2. The full turn of 360° shared by 8 equal angles gives 45° each.
3. Draw a line and mark the centre O on it. Construct a 90° angle at O with equal arcs.
4. Bisect the 90° angle: arcs from O cut the two arms at A and B, then equal arcs from A and B meet at C. OC makes 45° with each arm (SSS).
5. Extend the two arms and the bisector through O, and bisect one more right angle; this gives four lines, which is eight half-lines from O at 45° to each other.
Answer: Each angle is 45°; construct 90° and bisect it

maths_rules: Mark A and B on the arms with OA = OB.
A radius larger than OA, with arcs from A and from B on the far side of O, meets at C: AC = BC.

Extend CO beyond O to D inside angle AOB. Angle AOD + angle AOC = 180 degrees and angle BOD + angle BOC = 180 degrees.

media.description: A question from the book asks which other angles bisection can build and whether 65.5 degrees is one of them. Halving and adding give angles such as 135 and 67.5 degrees, and doubling shows that 65.5 degrees can never be reached.

video_script.why: The child can build ninety and forty five degrees and has not yet asked which other angles bisection reaches, or which it cannot reach.

<bookmark mark='m2'/>Bisection can build a right angle, and then half of it.

marks.m2: ninety is halved to forty five

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step one, halve the straight angle.
We halve, because bisection cuts an angle into two equal parts.
One hundred and eighty halved is ninety.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Halve ninety, and we get forty five.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Halve forty five, and we get twenty two and a half degrees.
beats.on_screen: Step 1: halve: 180 divided by 2 = 90; 90 divided by 2 = 45; 45 divided by 2 = 22.5

marks.m1: ninety and forty five are placed side by side
marks.m2: they make one hundred and thirty five
marks.m3: forty five and twenty two and a half make sixty seven and a half

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step two, place two built angles side by side.
Side by side, angles add up, so we get new angles.
Ninety and forty five together make one hundred and thirty five.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Forty five and twenty two and a half together make sixty seven and a half.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Many more angles can be built, and each one is made by halving and adding.

marks.m2: sixty seven and a half is doubled to one hundred and thirty five

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step three, double each built angle enough times.

Twenty two and a half, doubled twice, is ninety.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Sixty seven and a half, doubled once, is one hundred and thirty five.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>That is three forty fives.

One hundred and thirty one has neither, and twos do not help.

video_script.anchor: What other angles can be constructed using angle bisection? Can you construct a 65.5 degree angle?
video_script.design: One idea: halving and adding only reach angles that double into multiples of 45 degrees. The sixty degree and fifteen degree angles belong to a later topic and are not used here.
source: Figure it Out (angle bisection), Q4
never_show: the verdict on 65.5 before the answer line
maths_rules: Adding two built angles: 90 + 45 = 135, 45 + 22.5 = 67.5.
Every angle built by halving and adding is a whole multiple of 180 / 2^k, so doubled k times it is a whole multiple of 180, hence of 45.
65.5 x 2 = 131; further doublings give 131 x 2^n. A multiple of 45 needs the factors 3 and 5; 131 is prime, so 131 x 2^n has neither.
Check: 22.5 doubled twice is 90 = 2 x 45 and 67.5 doubled is 135 = 3 x 45, but 131 lies between 90 and 135 and is not a multiple of 45.
video_script.payoff_line: A sixty five and a half degree angle cannot be built by bisection

final_answer.value: Angles such as 90°, 45°, 22.5°, 135° and 67.5° can be made; 65.5° cannot, because no number of doublings turns it into a multiple of 45°
final_answer.spoken: angles such as ninety, forty five, twenty two and a half, one hundred and thirty five, and sixty seven and a half degrees can be made; sixty five and a half degrees cannot

video_script.substitution: The angles are built in the same way as the example in the book, by halving a right angle again and again, and by placing two built angles side by side.

media.teaching_notes: One idea: every angle made by halving and adding doubles into a whole multiple of 45 degrees, and 65.5 degrees does not. Watch for students who try to reach 65.5 degrees by repeated halving of a nearby angle.

interaction_points.answer: Angles such as 90°, 45°, 22.5°, 135° and 67.5° can be made; 65.5° cannot, because no number of doublings turns it into a multiple of 45°

maths_rules: Square ABCD: right angles at A and B by equal arcs, AD = BC = AB cut with the compass, and D joined to C.
Midpoints P, Q, R, S of AB, BC, CD, DA by perpendicular bisectors; the bisectors through P and R and through Q and S cross at the centre O.
PO = half of AB, because P is the midpoint of AB and PO is perpendicular to AB with O at half the height. PA = PB = half of AB too.
A semicircle with centre P and radius PA, inside the square, passes through A, B and O. The same holds for Q, R and S.
Two neighbouring semicircles, for example from P and from Q, overlap in a petal from O to B. Four such petals run from O to A, B, C and D.
A radius longer than half the side from P would cut the sides of the square beyond the corners, so the arc leaves the square.

content.text:
{{DIAGRAM:M2.S9.T9.C27.IMG1}}
$1$. Draw four angles of clearly different sizes, for example a small acute angle, a right angle made with equal arcs, a large acute angle and an obtuse angle.
$2$. For each angle with vertex $O$: with centre $O$ draw an arc that cuts the arms at $A$ and $B$, so $OA = OB$.
$3$. With one radius, draw arcs from $A$ and from $B$ that meet at $C$ inside the angle.
$4$. Join $OC$. It is the bisector, because $\triangle OAC$ is congruent to $\triangle OBC$ by $SSS$.
$5$. Check: fold the paper along $OC$; the two arms land on each other.
Answer: Each bisector is $OC$, where $OA = OB$ and $AC = BC$; $\triangle OAC$ is congruent to $\triangle OBC$ by $SSS$, so the two halves are equal

concepts.concept_name: Figure it out: Q2

content.text:
{{DIAGRAM:M2.S9.T9.C29.IMG1}}
$1$. Mark $A$ and $B$ on the arms with $OA = OB$.
$2$. With a radius larger than $OA$, draw equal arcs from $A$ and $B$ on the far side of $O$; they meet at $C$, with $AC = BC$.
$3$. In $\triangle OAC$ and $\triangle OBC$: $OA = OB$, $AC = BC$, and $OC$ is common.
$4$. So $\triangle OAC$ is congruent to $\triangle OBC$ by $SSS$, and $\angle AOC = \angle BOC$.
$5$. Extend $CO$ beyond $O$ to a point $D$ inside $\angle AOB$. $\angle AOD$ and $\angle AOC$ make a straight angle, and so do $\angle BOD$ and $\angle BOC$.
$6$. So $\angle AOD = 180^\circ - \angle AOC$ and $\angle BOD = 180^\circ - \angle BOC$; these are equal, so the line $CO$, extended beyond $O$, bisects $\angle AOB$.
Answer: Yes. $OA = OB$, $AC = BC$ and $OC$ is common, so $\triangle OAC$ is congruent to $\triangle OBC$ by $SSS$ and $\angle AOC = \angle BOC$; their supplements are equal too, so the line $CO$, extended beyond $O$, still bisects $\angle AOB$
steps: Mark A and B on the arms with OA = OB.
With a radius larger than OA, draw equal arcs from A and B on the far side of O; they meet at C, with AC = BC.
In ΔOAC and ΔOBC: OA = OB, AC = BC, and OC is common.
So ΔOAC ≅ ΔOBC by SSS, and ∠AOC = ∠BOC.
Extend CO beyond O to a point D inside ∠AOB. ∠AOD and ∠AOC make a straight angle, and so do ∠BOD and ∠BOC.
So ∠AOD = 180° − ∠AOC and ∠BOD = 180° − ∠BOC; these are equal, so the line CO, extended beyond O, bisects ∠AOB.

Mark $A$ and $B$ on the arms with $OA = OB$.
With a radius larger than $OA$, draw equal arcs from $A$ and $B$ on the far side of $O$; they meet at $C$, with $AC = BC$.
In $\triangle OAC$ and $\triangle OBC$: $OA = OB$, $AC = BC$, and $OC$ is common.
So $\triangle OAC$ is congruent to $\triangle OBC$ by $SSS$, and $\angle AOC = \angle BOC$.
Extend $CO$ beyond $O$ to a point $D$ inside $\angle AOB$. $\angle AOD$ and $\angle AOC$ make a straight angle, and so do $\angle BOD$ and $\angle BOC$.
So $\angle AOD = 180^\circ - \angle AOC$ and $\angle BOD = 180^\circ - \angle BOC$; these are equal, so the line $CO$, extended beyond $O$, bisects $\angle AOB$.

content.text:
$1$. From $180^\circ$ by halving: $90^\circ$. From $90^\circ$ by halving: $45^\circ$, $22.5^\circ$, and so on.
$2$. Sums of these also work, for example $90^\circ + 45^\circ = 135^\circ$ and $45^\circ + 22.5^\circ = 67.5^\circ$.
$3$. Every angle made this way, doubled enough times, becomes a whole multiple of $45^\circ$.
$4$. $65.5^\circ$ doubled is $131^\circ$, and every further doubling is $131^\circ$ times a power of $2$, which is never a multiple of $45^\circ$, because $131$ is not divisible by $3$ or by $5$.
$5$. So $65.5^\circ$ cannot be constructed by bisection.
$6$. Later in this chapter we build a $60^\circ$ angle; halving it gives $30^\circ$ and $15^\circ$, and sums such as $75^\circ$. Those all double into multiples of $15^\circ$, and $131^\circ$ times a power of $2$ is not one of them either.
Answer: Angles such as $90^\circ$, $45^\circ$, $22.5^\circ$, $135^\circ$ and $67.5^\circ$ can be made (and, once $60^\circ$ is built, $30^\circ$, $15^\circ$ and $75^\circ$); $65.5^\circ$ cannot, because no number of doublings turns it into a multiple of $45^\circ$, or even of $15^\circ$

content.text:
{{DIAGRAM:M2.S9.T9.C33.IMG1}}
$1$. Construct a square: a segment, right angles at both ends, equal sides cut with the compass, and join the fourth side.
$2$. Find the midpoint of each side by constructing its perpendicular bisector.
$3$. The two bisectors through opposite midpoints cross at the centre of the square.
$4$. With centre the midpoint of one side and radius half the side, draw a semicircle inside the square. It passes through the two corners at the ends of that side and through the centre.
$5$. Do the same from the other three midpoints. Each petal is where two semicircles overlap, from the centre to a corner.
$6$. These arcs just touch the sides of the square at the corners, so the petals are as large as they can be.
Answer: Find the midpoints of the four sides; from each midpoint draw a semicircle of radius half the side inside the square; the four petals run from the centre to the corners and are the largest possible

feedback: A changed radius on the second arc shows the copy too wide or too narrow, in red.

hint_ladder.text: Which two lengths do you need to carry from the given angle to the new ray?
Keep the same arc radius on both, then carry the chord length.
Set the compass on the two arc points of the given angle, then cut the new arc with it.
Same arc and same chord give congruent triangles by SSS, so the angles are equal.

content.text:
Repeating Units and Repeating Angles
Consider a design made of a row of five equal sectors (shapes with two equal straight arms and an arc), alternately pointing down and up, with neighbouring sectors sharing an arm. In this design, there is a single unit repeating itself. To construct this figure, we need to make exact copies of this unit in two different orientations.
In order to make exact copies, all the units must have the same arm lengths and the same angle between the arms. We can ensure equal arm lengths using a compass, but how do we ensure equal angles?
Let us develop a method to create an exact copy of a given angle.
Draw an angle. Create a copy of this angle using only a ruler and compass.
Steps of Construction to Copy an Angle
Draw an arc from A. This gives us three points that form the isosceles triangle ΔABC.
Draw an arc of the same radius from X.
Measure BC using a compass. Transfer this length on the arc from Z to get YZ = BC.
By the SSS congruence condition, ΔABC ≅ ΔXYZ. So, ∠A = ∠X.

concepts.concept_name: Copying an Angle: Q1

content.text:
{{DIAGRAM:M2.S11.T11.C37.IMG1}}
$1$. With centre $A$ and any radius, draw an arc that cuts the two arms at $B$ and $C$. Then $AB = AC$.
$2$. Draw a ray from $X$. With centre $X$ and the same radius, draw a long arc that cuts the ray at $Z$. Then $XZ = AB$.
$3$. Open the compass to the length $BC$.
$4$. With centre $Z$ and radius $BC$, cut the arc at $Y$. Then $YZ = BC$ and $XY = AC$.
$5$. Join $X$ and $Y$.
$6$. In $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle XYZ$: $AB = XZ$, $AC = XY$, $BC = ZY$. So $\triangle ABC$ is congruent to $\triangle XYZ$ by $SSS$, and $\angle YXZ = \angle CAB$.
Answer: $\angle YXZ$ is a copy of $\angle A$, because $\triangle ABC$ is congruent to $\triangle XYZ$ by $SSS$

Draw a ray from X. With centre X and the same radius, draw a long arc that cuts the ray at Z. Then XZ = AB.
Open the compass to the length BC.
With centre Z and radius BC, cut the arc at Y. Then YZ = BC and XY = AC.
Join X and Y.
In ΔABC and ΔXYZ: AB = XZ, AC = XY, BC = ZY. So ΔABC ≅ ΔXYZ by SSS, and ∠YXZ = ∠CAB.

content.question: An angle with vertex A is drawn. Copy it onto a ray from a point X using only a ruler and a compass, and justify that the copy is equal.
content.s_figure: The angle at A with an arc cutting its arms at B and C, an arc of the same radius from X cutting the ray at Z, the length BC marked off from Z to give Y, and the ray XY making the same angle as at A.
steps_tex:
{{DIAGRAM:M2.S11.T11.C37.IMG1}}
With centre $A$ and any radius, draw an arc that cuts the two arms at $B$ and $C$. Then $AB = AC$.
Draw a ray from $X$. With centre $X$ and the same radius, draw a long arc that cuts the ray at $Z$. Then $XZ = AB$.
Open the compass to the length $BC$.
With centre $Z$ and radius $BC$, cut the arc at $Y$. Then $YZ = BC$ and $XY = AC$.
Join $X$ and $Y$.
In $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle XYZ$: $AB = XZ$, $AC = XY$, $BC = ZY$. So $\triangle ABC$ is congruent to $\triangle XYZ$ by $SSS$, and $\angle YXZ = \angle CAB$.
content.answer_tex: $\angle YXZ$ is a copy of $\angle A$, because $\triangle ABC$ is congruent to $\triangle XYZ$ by $SSS$

$1$. With centre $A$ and any radius, draw an arc that cuts the two arms at $B$ and $C$. Then $AB = AC$.
$2$. Draw a ray from $X$. With centre $X$ and the same radius, draw a long arc that cuts the ray at $Z$. Then $XZ = AB$.
$3$. Open the compass to the length $BC$.
$4$. With centre $Z$ and radius $BC$, cut the arc at $Y$. Then $YZ = BC$ and $XY = AC$.
$5$. Join $X$ and $Y$.
$6$. In $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle XYZ$: $AB = XZ$, $AC = XY$, $BC = ZY$. So $\triangle ABC$ is congruent to $\triangle XYZ$ by $SSS$, and $\angle YXZ = \angle CAB$.

maths_rules: Each angle is drawn with the ruler only, facing a different way: upwards, sideways, downwards and slanting.
For each angle with corner A, an arc cuts the arms at B and C; the same radius from X cuts the new ray at Z.
The chord BC is carried from Z to give Y with ZY = BC; triangle ABC is congruent to triangle XZY by SSS.
So the angle at X equals the angle at A, whichever way the angle faces.

final_answer.value: For each angle, equal arcs from A and X and the chord BC moved to ZY give ΔABC ≅ ΔXZY by SSS, so every copy is equal to its angle
final_answer.spoken: each copy uses one radius and one chord, so the triangles match by side side side and every copy is equal to its angle

content.text:
{{DIAGRAM:M2.S12.T12.C39.IMG1}}
$1$. Draw four angles with the ruler only, each in a different direction on the page, for example one opening upwards, one sideways, one downwards and one slanting.
$2$. For each angle with vertex $A$: draw an arc from $A$, cutting the arms at $B$ and $C$.
$3$. Draw a new ray from a point $X$, and with the same radius draw an arc from $X$ cutting it at $Z$.
$4$. Open the compass to $BC$, and from $Z$ cut the arc at $Y$. Join $XY$.
$5$. Each copy is equal because $\triangle ABC$ is congruent to $\triangle XYZ$ by $SSS$. Check by laying tracing paper over both.
Answer: For each angle, equal arcs from $A$ and $X$ and the chord $BC$ moved to $ZY$ make $\triangle ABC$ congruent to $\triangle XYZ$ by $SSS$, so every copy equals its angle

maths_rules: Line l through B cuts m at A; l is the transversal.
An arc with centre A cuts m at C and l at D, between A and B: AC = AD.
The same radius with centre B cuts l at F, beyond B, away from A: BF = AD, and every point E on this arc has BE = AC.
The compass is set to CD; with centre F it cuts the arc at E, on the same side of l as C: FE = DC.
Triangle BFE is congruent to triangle ADC by SSS, so angle FBE = angle DAC. These are corresponding angles on the transversal l, so n through B and E is parallel to m.
Slip: E on the other side of l gives the angle in the opposite corner, and the line through B and E is not parallel to m.

content.text:
This procedure to copy an angle finds an important application in constructing parallel lines using only a ruler and compass.
Construction of a Line Parallel to the Given Line
Recall that we constructed equal corresponding angles to get parallel lines.
How do we implement this idea using a ruler and a compass?
Suppose there is a line m to which we need to draw a parallel line. We construct a line l that intersects m. Line l will serve as a transversal to line m and to the line parallel to m that we are going to construct.
Let us choose a point B on l through which we are going to draw the parallel line. This parallel line must make the same corresponding angle, as shown in the figure. This can be done by copying the angle between m and l.
Construct arcs of equal radius from A and B. Transfer the length CD to the arc from F (F is where the arc from B cuts l). These steps give a method to construct a line parallel to the given line.

content.text:
Worked example: A line m and a point B not on it are given. Construct a line through B parallel to m using only a ruler and a compass.
{{DIAGRAM:M2.S13.T13.C40.IMG2}}
1. Draw a line l through B that cuts m at A. l is the transversal.
2. With centre A and any radius, draw an arc that cuts m at C and cuts l at D, on the part of l between A and B.
3. With centre B and the same radius, draw an arc that cuts l at F, on the side of B away from A, as for the matching corner.
4. Open the compass to CD. With centre F, cut the arc at E, on the same side of l as C.
5. Draw the line n through B and E. ΔBFE ≅ ΔADC by SSS, so the angle at B equals the angle at A.
6. These are corresponding angles, so n is parallel to m.
Answer: The line n through B and E, since the copied corresponding angles are equal (SSS), so n ∥ m

maths_rules: Four lines m run in different directions: across, up and down, and two slanting ways. A point B is marked off each line.
A transversal l through B cuts m at A. An arc with centre A cuts m at C and l at D; the same radius with centre B cuts l at F, beyond B.
The chord CD is carried to F and cuts the arc at E, on the same side of l as C; n is drawn through B and E.
Triangle BFE is congruent to triangle ADC by SSS, so the corresponding angles at B and A are equal and n is parallel to m.
video_script.payoff_line: Each new line n is parallel to its line m

final_answer.value: Four pairs m and n, each made by copying the corresponding angle at A to B (SSS), so each n ∥ m
final_answer.spoken: for each line m, copy the corresponding angle at B, and each new line n is parallel to its line m, by side side side

video_script.substitution: Each pair is made in the same way as the example in the book: a transversal through B, equal arcs at A and B, and the chord carried across, only turned.

content.text:
{{DIAGRAM:M2.S14.T14.C43.IMG1}}
$1$. Draw four lines $m$ in different directions: across, up and down, and two slanting ways.
$2$. For each, mark a point $B$ off the line and draw a transversal $l$ through $B$ cutting $m$ at $A$.
$3$. Draw equal arcs from $A$ and from $B$. The arc from $A$ cuts $m$ at $C$ and $l$ at $D$; the arc from $B$ cuts $l$ at $F$, on the side of $B$ away from $A$. The chord $CD$ is transferred to the arc from $B$, starting at $F$ and on the same side of $l$ as $C$, to give $E$.
$4$. Draw $n$ through $B$ and $E$. $AD = BF$, $AC = BE$ and $DC = FE$, so $\triangle ADC$ is congruent to $\triangle BFE$ by $SSS$ and the corresponding angles are equal.
$5$. So each $n$ is parallel to its $m$.
Answer: Four pairs $m$ and $n$, each made by copying the corresponding angle at $A$ to $B$ by $SSS$, so each $n$ is parallel to $m$
steps: Draw four lines m in different directions: across, up and down, and two slanting ways.
For each, mark a point B off the line and draw a transversal l through B cutting m at A.

Draw equal arcs from A and from B. The arc from A cuts m at C and l at D; the arc from B cuts l at F, on the side of B away from A. The chord CD is transferred to the arc from B, starting at F and on the same side of l as C, to give E.
Draw n through B and E. AD = BF, AC = BE and DC = FE, so ΔADC ≅ ΔBFE by SSS and the corresponding angles are equal.
So each n is parallel to its m.

Draw equal arcs from $A$ and from $B$. The arc from $A$ cuts $m$ at $C$ and $l$ at $D$; the arc from $B$ cuts $l$ at $F$, on the side of $B$ away from $A$. The chord $CD$ is transferred to the arc from $B$, starting at $F$ and on the same side of $l$ as $C$, to give $E$.
Draw $n$ through $B$ and $E$. $AD = BF$, $AC = BE$ and $DC = FE$, so $\triangle ADC$ is congruent to $\triangle BFE$ by $SSS$ and the corresponding angles are equal.
So each $n$ is parallel to its $m$.

maths_rules: Each angle of an equilateral triangle is 60 degrees.
At O, six such angles meet, and 6 x 60 = 360, the full angle round a point, so there is no gap and no overlap.
The six outer sides are sides of congruent triangles, so they are all equal.
At each outer corner two angles of 60 degrees meet, making 60 + 60 = 120 degrees, so all six angles are equal.
Equal sides and equal angles make the outer figure a regular hexagon.

maths_rules: Angles AOB, BOC and COD are angles of equilateral triangles, so each is 60 degrees.
Angle AOD = angle AOB + angle BOC + angle COD = 60 + 60 + 60 = 180 degrees; added in steps: 60 + 60 = 120, 120 + 60 = 180.
An angle of 180 degrees is a straight angle, so OA and OD point in opposite directions and AOD is a straight line.
In the same way angle BOE = 180 degrees and angle COF = 180 degrees, so BOE and COF are straight lines too.

topics.summary: Angles round a point add to 360°; six 60° angles fill it, so six equilateral triangles make a regular hexagon.

content.text:
Regular Hexagons
Recall that a regular polygon has equal sides and equal angles. A regular polygon with 3 sides is an equilateral triangle, and a regular polygon with 4 sides is a square. We have constructed these figures earlier.
Constructing a regular hexagon is within our reach! Can we break a regular hexagon into smaller pieces that can be constructed?
Regular Hexagon and Equilateral Triangles
What happens when we join the 'opposite' points of a regular hexagon? Since a regular hexagon has equal sides and angles, can we expect a figure like this? Will all the triangles in the figure be equilateral triangles?
To answer these questions, we will reverse our approach. Can six congruent equilateral triangles be placed together as in the figure? If yes, will it result in a regular hexagon?
If six congruent equilateral triangles can indeed be placed as shown in the figure, then the sides of the resulting hexagon are equal, and their angles are 60 + 60 = 120° (how?). So what we really need to examine is whether 6 congruent equilateral triangles can fit this way without overlapping and without leaving any gaps around the centre.
We have defined a degree by taking the complete angle around a point to be 360°. So all the angles around the centre should add up to 360°.
Since each angle in an equilateral triangle is 60°, six such angles add up to 360°. Therefore, six congruent triangles can be arranged as shown.

concepts.concept_name: A Regular Hexagon from Six Triangles: Q1

content.text:
$1$. All the angles round a point add up to $360^\circ$.
$2$. $40^\circ + 60^\circ + 50^\circ + 30^\circ + 40^\circ + 90^\circ +$ gap angle $= 360^\circ$.
$3$. The six known angles add to $310^\circ$.
$4$. So the gap angle is $360^\circ - 310^\circ = 50^\circ$.
$5$. $70^\circ$ is more than $50^\circ$, so the $70^\circ$ angle would overlap its neighbours.
Answer: The gap is $50^\circ$, so the $70^\circ$ angle does not fit
steps: All the angles round a point add up to 360°.

So the gap angle is 360° − 310° = 50°.
70° is more than 50°, so the 70° angle would overlap its neighbours.
content.answer: The gap is 50°, so the 70° angle does not fit

concepts.concept_name: A Regular Hexagon from Six Triangles: Q2

content.text:
{{DIAGRAM:M3.S16.T16.C51.IMG1}}
$1$. At $O$, $\angle AOB$, $\angle BOC$ and $\angle COD$ are angles of equilateral triangles, so each is $60^\circ$.
$2$. $\angle AOD = \angle AOB + \angle BOC + \angle COD = 60^\circ + 60^\circ + 60^\circ = 180^\circ$.
$3$. An angle of $180^\circ$ is a straight angle, so $OA$ and $OD$ point in opposite directions: $AOD$ is a straight line.
$4$. In the same way $\angle BOE = 180^\circ$ and $\angle COF = 180^\circ$.
$5$. So $BOE$ and $COF$ are straight lines too.
Answer: Each of $\angle AOD$, $\angle BOE$ and $\angle COF$ is three $60^\circ$ angles, which is $180^\circ$, a straight angle
steps: At O, ∠AOB, ∠BOC and ∠COD are angles of equilateral triangles, so each is 60°.
An angle of 180° is a straight angle, so OA and OD point in opposite directions: AOD is a straight line.
In the same way ∠BOE = 180° and ∠COF = 180°.
So BOE and COF are straight lines too.
content.answer: Each of ∠AOD, ∠BOE and ∠COF is three 60° angles, which is 180°, a straight angle

video_script.anchor: A segment AX with the point A marked, a ruler and a compass.
video_script.design: One segment, one compass opening, two arcs and a triangle with three equal sides. The sides are drawn equal only because they are radii. The slip is a smaller second arc.
source: Construct a 60° angle at A on a segment AX using only a rule
video_script.wrong_move: Kiko draws the second arc from B with a smaller radius. Then BC is shorter than AB, the triangle is not equilateral, and the angle is not sixty degrees.
maths_rules: AB = AC, because both are radii of the first arc.
BA = BC, because both are radii of the second arc, which has the same radius.
So AB = BC = CA and triangle ABC is equilateral.
Each angle of an equilateral triangle is 60°, so ∠CAX = 60°.
Slip: a smaller radius from B makes BC shorter than AB, so the triangle is not equilateral.

content.text:
We can construct a regular hexagon more directly if we can construct a 120° angle using a ruler and a compass. How do we do it? This can be done if we can construct a 60° angle.
Construction of a 60° angle
How do we construct a 60° angle? We get a 60° angle if we construct an equilateral triangle! We can use the following steps for this.
Suppose we need a 60° angle at point A on a line segment AX.
Step 1: Construct an arc with centre A and any radius. (It cuts AX at B.)
Step 2: With the same radius, cut another arc from B that meets the first arc. Let C be the point at which the arcs meet. We have ∠CAX = 60°.
Why is ∠CAX = 60°? Is there an equilateral triangle here?

content.text:
1. Predict first: which triangle has every angle equal to 60°?
2. An arc with centre A cuts AX at B; an arc of the same radius from B meets it at C.
3. AB = AC (radii from A) and BA = BC (radii from B), so all three sides are equal.
4. ABC is equilateral, so each angle is 60°, and ∠CAX = ∠CAB = 60°.

content.text:
1. Predict first: a 60° angle sits on a straight line. What is the angle next to it on the line?
2. 60° next to it on a straight line leaves 180° − 60° = 120°; or put two 60° angles side by side.
3. A regular hexagon is six equilateral triangles round a centre, so a circle with radius equal to the side carries all six corners.
4. Step the compass, set to the side length, six times round the circle; it closes exactly.

content.text:
Worked example: Construct a 120° angle at a point A on a line, using only a ruler and a compass.
{{DIAGRAM:M3.S17.T17.C53.IMG2}}
1. Draw a line and mark A on it. Mark X on the line to the right of A.
2. With centre A and any radius, draw a large arc that cuts AX at B.
3. With centre B and the same radius, cut the arc at C. Then ∠CAB = 60°.
4. With centre C and the same radius, cut the arc again at D. Then ∠DAC = 60°, by the same equilateral triangle reason.
5. Join A and D. ∠DAX = 60° + 60° = 120°.
6. Check: D lies on the side away from X, and the angle between AD and the line on the left is 180° − 120° = 60°.
Answer: ∠DAX = 120°, made of two 60° angles from equilateral triangles

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>This is a question from your book.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>A six sided shape with equal sides and equal angles is called a regular hexagon.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step one, open the compass to four centimetres against the ruler.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Draw a circle with centre O, and mark a point eigh on it.
So every point on the circle is four centimetres from O.
beats.on_screen: Step 1: compass opened to 4 cm on the ruler; circle with centre O; A marked on it

marks.m1: B is cut on the circle
marks.m2: triangle O A B is shaded and its three sides are marked equal

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step two, with centre eigh and radius four centimetres, cut the circle at B.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Triangle O eigh B has three sides of four centimetres.
So it is equilateral, and angle eigh O B is sixty degrees.
beats.on_screen: Step 2: centre A, radius 4 cm, cuts the circle at B; OA = OB = AB = 4 cm, so triangle OAB is equilateral and ∠AOB = 60°

marks.m1: C, D, E and F are cut one after another
marks.m2: six sixty degree angles at O fill the full turn

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step three, keep the same opening and cut C from B, then D, E and F.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Six angles of sixty degrees make three hundred and sixty degrees, a full turn.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>So the next step from F lands back on eigh.
beats.on_screen: Step 3: with the same opening, cut C from B, D from C, E from D, F from E. 6 × 60° = 360°, so the next step lands back on A

marks.m1: the six points are joined in order

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step four, join eigh, B, C, D, E and F in order.
Every side is four centimetres.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>At each corner two triangles meet, so each angle is sixty plus sixty.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>The hexagon eigh B C D E F has six equal sides and six equal angles.

narration: <bookmark mark='a'/>Kiko has one question to ask.
What is the real-life use case?
<bookmark mark='b'/>This shape is found in a beehive.
The front face of a honeycomb is made of hexagonal cells.
Bees keep eggs safe and store food in these cells.
The cells fit together with no gaps, so no space is wasted.
beats.on_screen: Kiko at bottom right, blue question box beside him with the question, then the photo of the honeycomb beside a regular hexagon Photo: A honeycomb with bees on hexagonal cells

marks.a: Kiko and the blue question box appear

narration: <bookmark mark='a'/>Kiko has one question to ask.
What mistake do some students make here?
<bookmark mark='b'/>Some students think we can change the compass opening for each cut, because the circle is already drawn.
Then the next side would not be four centimetres, because the radius changed.
The sides would not be equal, so it is not a regular hexagon.
The compass must keep the same opening for every cut.
beats.on_screen: Kiko at bottom right, blue question box beside him with the question, then a changed compass opening giving an uneven shape, crossed out, then the same opening giving a regular hexagon

source: Construct a regular hexagon with side 4 cm using a ruler and
maths_rules: Compass set to 4 cm with the ruler; circle with centre O; A on the circle.
OA = OB = AB = 4 cm, so triangle OAB is equilateral and angle AOB = 60°.
Five more cuts of 4 cm give C, D, E, F; each triangle at O is equilateral with angle 60°.
6 x 60° = 360°, so the next step from F lands back on A.
Each side is 4 cm; each corner angle is 60° + 60° = 120°.
video_script.payoff_line: Each side is four centimetres and each angle is one hundred and twenty degrees.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>This is a question from your book.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>We want a six sided shape with equal sides and equal angles.
Each side is five centimetres, and we start with the side eigh B.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>We have a ruler and a compass.
We know how to build a one hundred and twenty degree angle.
How can we use it?

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>A six sided shape with equal sides and equal angles is called a regular hexagon.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Each of its angles is one hundred and twenty degrees.
We make that from two steps of sixty degrees.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Given, each side is five centimetres, and we have a ruler and a compass.

marks.m1: the line to find is written

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>We have to construct the regular hexagon.
beats.on_screen: To find: the regular hexagon

marks.m1: A B is drawn five centimetres long
marks.m2: two equal arcs at B make the angle and C is cut on the ray

beats.colours: the two arcs in two colours
narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step one, draw eigh B as five centimetres with the ruler.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>At B, build one hundred and twenty degrees from two equal arcs.
Then cut B C as five centimetres on the new ray.
We need that angle, because every corner of a regular hexagon has it.
beats.on_screen: Step 1: AB = 5 cm. At B build 120° from two 60° arcs; cut BC = 5 cm

marks.m1: the same angle is built at C in the same direction
marks.m2: D, E and F are cut in turn, each side five centimetres

beats.colours: each new corner in the same colour
narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step two, build the same angle at C, and turn the same way as before.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Cut C D as five centimetres.
Repeat at D and at E to get E and F.
We turn the same way, so the path bends round and closes.
beats.on_screen: Step 2: at C, then D, then E, build 120° in the same direction. CD = DE = EF = 5 cm

marks.m1: F is joined to A and the hexagon is closed

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step three, join F to eigh.
So the path closes into a six sided shape.
beats.on_screen: Step 3: join F to A

marks.m1: the ruler is placed along F A
marks.m2: the last side reads the same as the others

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step four, check.
Place the ruler along F eigh.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>It reads five centimetres, the same as the other sides, so the shape is regular.
beats.on_screen: Step 4, check: FA measured with the ruler = 5 cm

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>The hexagon eigh B C D E F is regular.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>The shape has six sides of five centimetres and six angles of one hundred and twenty degrees.

narration: <bookmark mark='a'/>Kiko has one question to ask.
What is the real-life use case?
<bookmark mark='b'/>A tiler lays hexagonal tiles on a courtyard floor.
Every tile has six equal sides and six equal angles.
The corners fit together with no gap, so the floor is covered neatly.
beats.on_screen: Kiko at bottom right, blue question box beside him with the question, then the photo of the hexagon tiles beside a regular hexagon Photo: Hexagonal tiles laid on a courtyard floor

narration: <bookmark mark='a'/>Kiko has one question to ask.
What mistake do some students make here?
<bookmark mark='b'/>Some students think at C we can turn the other way, because the angle looks the same.
Then the path bends back across the sides we already drew.
It would not close into a hexagon, because the corners do not go round in order.
At every corner we must turn the same way.

maths_rules: Draw AB = 5 cm with the ruler.
At B build 120° from two 60° equal arcs, on the same side each time; cut BC = 5 cm.
Repeat at C, D and E in the same direction to get D, E and F with CD = DE = EF = 5 cm.
Join F to A. Check: FA measures 5 cm with the ruler.
Slip: turning the other way at one corner bends the path back, so it does not close.

content.text:
{{DIAGRAM:M3.S18.T18.C56.IMG1}}
$1$. Open the compass to $4\text{ cm}$ using the ruler, and draw a circle with centre $O$.
$2$. Mark a point $A$ on the circle.
$3$. With centre $A$ and radius $4\text{ cm}$, cut the circle at $B$. $\triangle OAB$ is equilateral, so $\angle AOB = 60^\circ$.
$4$. With centre $B$, cut the circle at $C$; with centre $C$, cut at $D$; then $E$ and $F$ in the same way.
$5$. Six angles of $60^\circ$ at $O$ make $360^\circ$, so the sixth step lands back on $A$.
$6$. Join $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$, $E$, $F$ in order. Every side is $4\text{ cm}$ and every angle is $60^\circ + 60^\circ = 120^\circ$.
Answer: $ABCDEF$, with six sides of $4\text{ cm}$ and six angles of $120^\circ$

concepts.concept_name: Constructing 60°, 120° and a Regular Hexagon: Q2

content.text:
{{DIAGRAM:M3.S18.T18.C58.IMG1}}
$1$. With centre $A$ and any radius, draw a long arc that cuts $AX$ at $B$.
$2$. With centre $B$ and the same radius, draw an arc that cuts the first arc at $C$.
$3$. Join $A$ and $C$. $\angle CAX$ is the required angle.
$4$. Join $B$ and $C$. $AB = AC$, because both are radii of the first arc.
$5$. $BA = BC$, because both are radii of the second arc, which has the same radius.
$6$. So $AB = BC = CA$: $\triangle ABC$ is equilateral, and each of its angles is $60^\circ$. So $\angle CAX = 60^\circ$.
Answer: $\angle CAX = 60^\circ$, because $\triangle ABC$ has three equal sides and so is equilateral
steps: With centre A and any radius, draw a long arc that cuts AX at B.
With centre B and the same radius, draw an arc that cuts the first arc at C.
Join A and C. ∠CAX is the required angle.
Join B and C. AB = AC, because both are radii of the first arc.
BA = BC, because both are radii of the second arc, which has the same radius.
So AB = BC = CA: ΔABC is equilateral, and each of its angles is 60°. So ∠CAX = 60°.

concepts.concept_name: Constructing 60°, 120° and a Regular Hexagon: Q3

content.text:
{{DIAGRAM:M3.S18.T18.C60.IMG1}}
$1$. Draw $AB = 5\text{ cm}$ with the ruler.
$2$. At $B$, construct $120^\circ$ between $BA$ and a new ray: two $60^\circ$ steps with equal arcs. Cut the ray at $C$ with $BC = 5\text{ cm}$.
$3$. At $C$, construct $120^\circ$ in the same way, turning the same direction, and cut $CD = 5\text{ cm}$.
$4$. Repeat at $D$ and $E$ to get $E$ and $F$ with $DE = EF = 5\text{ cm}$.
$5$. Join $F$ to $A$. The angles of a regular hexagon add to $6 \times 120 = 720$ degrees, and $FA$ comes out $5\text{ cm}$.
$6$. All six sides are $5\text{ cm}$ and all six angles are $120^\circ$.
Answer: $ABCDEF$, with six sides of $5\text{ cm}$ and six angles of $120^\circ$
steps: Draw AB = 5 cm with the ruler.

At C, construct 120° in the same way, turning the same direction, and cut CD = 5 cm.
Repeat at D and E to get E and F with DE = EF = 5 cm.
Join F to A. The angles of a regular hexagon add to 6 × 120 = 720 degrees, and FA comes out 5 cm.
All six sides are 5 cm and all six angles are 120°.

tool_config.idea: An arc from P cuts line l at two points that are equally far from P; the perpendicular bisector of those two points passes through P and is at 90° to l. Halving 60° and 30° gives 30° and 15°.
tool_config.title: Outside Point Drop Line
tool_config.screen: A line l and a point P off it; a compass and ruler; steps: arc from P cutting l twice, equal arcs from the two cut points, join to P; an angle readout; an angle mode for 60°, 30° and 15°.
feedback: An arc that does not reach l shows no cut points and asks for a bigger radius.
A correct perpendicular shows the 90° mark and the two congruent triangles.
In angle mode the halves are shown equal with the SSS triangles shaded.
tool_config.done_when: Six challenges done with the readouts correct.
challenges: Draw the perpendicular from P to a horizontal l.
P close to l: draw the perpendicular.
l slanting: draw the perpendicular from P.
An arc too small to reach l: see what goes wrong.
Construct 30° by halving 60°.
Construct 15° by halving 30°.

hint_ladder.text: Which two points on l are the same distance from P?
An arc from P gives them; their perpendicular bisector goes through P.
From the two cut points draw equal arcs that cross on the side away from P.
Join the crossing to P: P is equally far from both cut points, so the line meets l at 90°.

student_does: Draw an arc from P that cuts l at two points.
From the two points draw equal arcs that cross on the far side.
Join the crossing to P and read the angle with l.
In angle mode, build 60° and halve it once and twice.

video_script.wrong_move: Kiko draws the arcs from B and from C with different radii. Then BD and CD are not equal, the two triangles do not match, and AD does not cut the angle in half.
maths_rules: Centre A, any radius, cut the line at B. Centre B, same radius, cut the arc at C. Triangle ABC is equilateral, so ∠CAB = 60°.
Bisect ∠CAB: arcs from B and from C with one radius meet at D inside the angle. Join A and D.
AB = AC (radii of one arc), BD = CD (one radius), AD is common, so triangle ABD is congruent to triangle ACD by SSS.
So ∠DAB = ∠DAC, and each is half of 60°, which is 30°.
Slip: arcs of different radii make BD unequal to CD, so the triangles do not match.

video_script.wrong_move: Kiko reads angle AGH as the same angle as the hexagon, so it would be 120 degrees. But angle AGH and angle LGH lie on a straight line and add to 180 degrees, so angle AGH is 60 degrees.
maths_rules: GHIJKL is a regular hexagon, so each of its angles is 120°.
AG lies along the extended side LG and AH along the extended side IH.
∠AGH + ∠LGH = 180° (straight line), so ∠AGH = 180° − 120° = 60°.
In the same way ∠AHG = 180° − 120° = 60°.
The angles of a triangle add to 180°, so ∠GAH = 180° − 60° − 60° = 60°.
All three angles are 60°, so triangle AGH is equilateral; the same reasoning works for the other five points.
Slip: reading ∠AGH as the hexagon angle 120°.

content.text:
1. Predict first: the middle of the star is a hexagon GHIJKL. What is each of its angles?
2. Construct a regular hexagon GHIJKL and extend each side both ways.
3. Each angle of the hexagon is 120°; the angle next to it on a straight line is 180° − 120° = 60°.
4. Each point triangle has two 60° base angles, so its third angle is 60° too: it is equilateral.

What is the real-life use case?

narration: <bookmark mark='a'/>Kiko has one question to ask.
What mistake do some students make here?
<bookmark mark='b'/>Some students think we can draw the arcs from B and D, because both are on the arms.
But eigh D is not equal to eigh B, so the two triangles do not match.
The line would not cut the angle in half.
The two points must be the same distance from eigh, so we use B and E.

video_script.design: One line, one point A and the arcs from the last video. A new pair of arcs sits inside the thirty degree angle. The slip is drawing from D instead of E.
source: Construct a 15° angle at a point A on a line, using only a r
video_script.wrong_move: Kiko draws the arcs from B and D. But AD is not equal to AB, so the two triangles do not match and AF does not cut the angle in half.
maths_rules: Construct ∠CAB = 60° with two equal arcs and bisect it, giving ray AD with ∠DAB = 30°.
The first arc from A cuts AD at a point E, so AB = AE (radii of one arc).
Arcs from B and E with one radius meet at F inside ∠DAB. Join A and F.
AB = AE, BF = EF, AF is common, so triangle ABF is congruent to triangle AEF by SSS.
So ∠FAB = ∠FAE, and each is half of 30°, which is 15°.
Slip: arcs from B and D, where AD is not equal to AB, do not give matching triangles.
video_script.payoff_line: Angle F eigh B is fifteen degrees.

final_answer.spoken: angle F eigh B is fifteen degrees

video_script.substitution: The first arc from A cuts both arms at the same distance, so AB equals AE.

media.teaching_notes: One idea: the same cutting in half works again on the thirty degree angle, with arcs from points at equal distance from A. Watch for students who draw the arc from a point not on the arm at that distance.

content.text:
{{DIAGRAM:M3.S20.T20.C65.IMG1}}
$1$. With centre $A$ and any radius, draw an arc that cuts the line at $B$.
$2$. With centre $B$ and the same radius, cut the arc at $C$. Then $\angle CAB = 60^\circ$, because $\triangle ABC$ is equilateral.
$3$. Now bisect $\angle CAB$: with one radius, draw arcs from $B$ and from $C$ that meet at $D$ inside the angle.
$4$. Join $A$ and $D$.
$5$. $AB = AC$, $BD = CD$ and $AD$ is common, so $\triangle ABD$ is congruent to $\triangle ACD$ by $SSS$.
$6$. So $\angle DAB = \angle DAC$, and each is half of $60^\circ$, which is $30^\circ$.
Answer: $\angle DAB = 30^\circ$: a $60^\circ$ angle from an equilateral triangle, bisected using $SSS$

With centre B and the same radius, cut the arc at C. Then ∠CAB = 60° (ΔABC is equilateral).
Now bisect ∠CAB: with one radius, draw arcs from B and from C that meet at D inside the angle.
Join A and D.
AB = AC, BD = CD and AD is common, so ΔABD ≅ ΔACD by SSS.
So ∠DAB = ∠DAC, and each is half of 60°, which is 30°.

content.text:
{{DIAGRAM:M3.S20.T20.C67.IMG1}}
$1$. The inner figure $GHIJKL$ is a regular hexagon, so each of its angles is $120^\circ$.
$2$. In $\triangle AGH$, side $GH$ is a side of the hexagon, and $AG$ and $AH$ lie along the extended sides $LG$ and $IH$.
$3$. $\angle AGH$ and $\angle LGH$ make a straight angle, so $\angle AGH = 180^\circ - 120^\circ = 60^\circ$.
$4$. In the same way $\angle AHG = 180^\circ - 120^\circ = 60^\circ$.
$5$. The angles of a triangle add to $180^\circ$, so $\angle GAH = 180^\circ - 60^\circ - 60^\circ = 60^\circ$.
$6$. All three angles are $60^\circ$, so $\triangle AGH$ is equilateral; the same reasoning works for the other five points.
Answer: Yes. Each base angle is $180^\circ - 120^\circ = 60^\circ$, so all three angles are $60^\circ$ and each point is an equilateral triangle

content.text:
{{DIAGRAM:M3.S21.T21.C69.IMG1}}
$1$. With centre $P$ and a radius large enough, draw an arc that cuts $l$ at two points $X$ and $Y$. Then $PX = PY$.
$2$. $P$ is equally far from $X$ and $Y$, so $P$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $XY$.
$3$. With centres $X$ and $Y$ and one radius, draw arcs on the other side of $l$ that meet at $Q$. Then $QX = QY$.
$4$. Join $P$ and $Q$; $PQ$ meets $l$ at $O$.
$5$. $\triangle PXQ$ is congruent to $\triangle PYQ$ by $SSS$, so $\angle XPO = \angle YPO$; then $\triangle POX$ is congruent to $\triangle POY$ by $SAS$, so $\angle POX = \angle POY = 90^\circ$.
$6$. So $PQ$ is the perpendicular to $l$ through $P$.
Answer: Cut $l$ at $X$ and $Y$ with an arc from $P$, then find $Q$ with $QX = QY$; $PQ$ is the perpendicular bisector of $XY$, using $SSS$ and then $SAS$, so it is perpendicular to $l$ and passes through $P$
steps: With centre P and a radius large enough, draw an arc that cuts l at two points X and Y. Then PX = PY.
P is equally far from X and Y, so P lies on the perpendicular bisector of XY.
With centres X and Y and one radius, draw arcs on the other side of l that meet at Q. Then QX = QY.
Join P and Q; PQ meets l at O.
ΔPXQ ≅ ΔPYQ by SSS, so ∠XPO = ∠YPO; then ΔPOX ≅ ΔPOY by SAS, so ∠POX = ∠POY = 90°.
So PQ is the perpendicular to l through P.

content.text:
6.2 Tiling
Covering a region using a set of shapes, without gaps or overlaps, is called tiling.
Consider a rectangular grid made of unit squares. We call this a 4 × 6 grid, since it has 4 rows and 6 columns.
Can a 4 × 6 grid be tiled using multiple copies of 2 × 1 tiles? We are allowed to rotate a 2 × 1 tile and use it. (Vertical tile, horizontal tile.)
Here is one way. This is not the only tiling possible.
Can a 4 × 7 grid be tiled using 2 × 1 tiles?

1. Predict first: which matters more, the number of rows or the number of columns?
2. If the number of rows is even, every column fills with vertical tiles.

4. If both are odd, m × n is odd, so it can never be tiled.

Students decide whether an m × n grid can be tiled with 2 × 1 tiles when both sides are even, one is even, or both are odd, and give a strategy or a reason.
Students tile grids of different sizes with 2 × 1 tiles, or show by counting that a grid cannot be tiled.

segments.summary: Each 2 × 1 tile covers two squares, so an odd number of squares can never be tiled; an even side makes it easy.
segments.brief_summary: Each 2 × 1 tile covers two squares, so an odd number of squares can never be tiled; an even side makes it easy.

media.context: Constructions and Tilings. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: A grid of four rows and seven columns. The squares count to an even number, and every column holds four squares, so two upright tiles fill each column. Keeko's doubt, that an odd number of columns spoils it, is struck.

video_script.why: The child sees that a grid with an odd number of columns can still be tiled when each column has an even length.

video_script.anchor: A grid of unit squares with m rows and n columns, where one of m and n is even and the other is odd, and a tile that covers 2 squares.
video_script.design: One general grid with one even side. The tiles go along that side, upright for even columns, lying for even rows. The slip is giving up at the odd side.
source: Is an m × n grid tileable with 2 × 1 tiles if one of m and n
hold_back: horizontal tiles along rows of even length
video_script.wrong_move: Kiko thinks one odd side spoils it. But only upright tiles were tried. Lying tiles along a row of even length also work.
maths_rules: If the number of rows m is even, cover each column with vertical tiles.
If instead the number of columns n is even, each row has an even number of squares.
Then cover each row with n ÷ 2 horizontal tiles.
Example: a 3 × 4 grid, each of the 3 rows takes 2 horizontal tiles, 6 tiles in all.
Slip: one odd side does not spoil the tiling; use the even side.
video_script.payoff_line: Yes, use vertical tiles down the even columns, or horizontal tiles along rows of even length.

final_answer.value: Yes: use vertical tiles along the even side's columns, or horizontal tiles along rows of even length

content.text:
$1$. The grid has $5 \times 7 = 35$ squares of side $1\text{ unit}$.
$2$. Each tile covers exactly $2$ squares of side $1\text{ unit}$, with no overlap.
$3$. So any number of tiles covers an even number of squares.
$4$. $35$ is odd, so it is not a number of squares that tiles can cover exactly.
$5$. So there is no tiling of the $5 \times 7$ grid.
Answer: Not possible: tiles always cover an even number of squares, and $35$ is odd

content.text:
What about this one? Were you able to tile this? How can we be sure that this is not tileable?
Can you find another unit square that, when removed from a 5 × 3 grid, makes it non-tileable?
There is an interesting way to look at these questions. For any tiling problem of this kind, we can create a similar problem with the unit squares coloured black and white so that black squares have only white neighbours and white squares have only black neighbours.
In the black-and-white region, the problem is to tile the region with the 2 × 1 black-and-white tiles so that each black square of a tile sits on a black square of the grid, and each white square sits on a white square.
If the plain grid is tileable, is the black-and-white-grid tileable? If the black-and-white grid is tileable, is the plain grid tileable? It can be seen that the answer to both the questions is yes.
Is the black-and-white region tileable?
Any region tiled with black-and-white-tiles must have an equal number of black tiles and white tiles.
Since the black-and-white region has 8 white squares and 6 black squares, it can never be tiled with these tiles!
Use this idea to find another unit square that, when removed from a 5 × 3 grid, makes it non-tileable?
Isn't it surprising how, by introducing colours and making the problem more complicated, it becomes easier to tackle? What a creative way of looking at the problem!

Can you find another unit square that, when removed from a 5 × 3 grid, makes it non-tileable?

There is an interesting way to look at these questions. For any tiling problem of this kind, we can create a similar problem with the unit squares coloured black and white so that black squares have only white neighbours and white squares have only black neighbours.

In the black-and-white region, the problem is to tile the region with the 2 × 1 black-and-white tiles so that each black square of a tile sits on a black square of the grid, and each white square sits on a white square.
If the plain grid is tileable, is the black-and-white-grid tileable? If the black-and-white grid is tileable, is the plain grid tileable? It can be seen that the answer to both the questions is yes.
Is the black-and-white region tileable?
Any region tiled with black-and-white-tiles must have an equal number of black tiles and white tiles.
Since the black-and-white region has 8 white squares and 6 black squares, it can never be tiled with these tiles!
Use this idea to find another unit square that, when removed from a 5 × 3 grid, makes it non-tileable?

content.text:
1. Predict first: the grid with the top middle square removed has 14 squares. Can it be tiled?
2. Colour the grid like a chessboard, with the corners white: 8 white and 7 black squares.
3. A 2 × 1 tile always covers two neighbouring squares, one white and one black.
4. Remove a black square and 8 white and 6 black are left; 7 tiles would need 7 of each, so it is impossible.

maths_rules: With white corners, the 5 × 3 grid has 8 white and 7 black squares.
Each tile covers one white and one black square, so the colours left must be equal.
Removing any black square leaves 8 white and 6 black, which no set of tiles can cover.
A square is black when its row number plus its column number is odd.
Besides the top middle square, these are: row 2 column 1, row 2 column 3, row 3 column 2, row 4 column 1, row 4 column 3, row 5 column 2.
Example: removing the square in row 2, column 1 makes the grid untileable.

content.text:
{{DIAGRAM:M4.S25.T25.C94.IMG1}}
$1$. With white corners, the full $5 \times 3$ grid has $8$ white and $7$ black squares.
$2$. The top middle square sits between two white corners, so it is black.
$3$. After removing it, $8$ white and $6$ black squares are left.
$4$. Each $2 \times 1$ tile covers two neighbouring squares, and neighbours have different colours, so each tile covers one white and one black.
$5$. $7$ tiles would cover $7$ white and $7$ black squares, but there are $8$ white and $6$ black.
$6$. So no tiling exists.
Answer: Not tileable: $8$ white and $6$ black squares remain, but every tile covers one of each

content.text:
{{DIAGRAM:M4.S25.T25.C96.IMG1}}
$1$. Colour the $5 \times 3$ grid with white corners: $8$ white and $7$ black squares.
$2$. Removing any black square leaves $8$ white and $6$ black, which no set of tiles can cover.
$3$. The black squares are the ones whose row number plus column number is odd.
$4$. Besides the top middle square, these are: row $2$, column $1$; row $2$, column $3$; row $3$, column $2$; row $4$, column $1$; row $4$, column $3$; row $5$, column $2$.
$5$. For example, removing the square in row $2$, column $1$ makes the grid non-tileable.
Answer: Any black square works, for example row $2$, column $1$; the others are row $2$ column $3$, row $3$ column $2$, row $4$ column $1$, row $4$ column $3$ and row $5$ column $2$

content.text:
{{DIAGRAM:M4.S26.T26.C98.IMG1}}
$1$. $12$ squares need $4$ tiles of $3$ squares.
$2$. One way: cover the top left square with an $L$ that also covers the square beside it and the square below it, in rows $1$ and $2$.
$3$. Then row $2$, column $2$ is left in the top part; cover it with row $3$, columns $2$ and $3$, in an $L$.
$4$. Row $3$, column $1$ goes with row $4$, columns $1$ and $2$, in an $L$.
$5$. Row $3$, column $4$ goes with row $4$, columns $3$ and $4$, in an $L$.
$6$. All $12$ squares are covered by $4$ tiles, with no gaps and no overlaps.
Answer: Yes, it is possible: four $L$ tiles, turned to different positions
